
=================================================================
#45 Seohyun  (593)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Chunchu Era · place: daeya · tone: forbidden romance into cavern legend
Logline: Before there is a Yushin there is a road, and a young man on it who should be looking where he is going.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Before there is a Yushin there is a road, and a young man on it who should be looking where he is going.
[1] [MAP 593: ]
[2] ¶ Kim Seohyun is the son of Gaya’s last prince. In the capital, that’s the kind of fact people bring up just after he leaves the room. His father rode in the cart that handed the kingdom over, then spent his life proving it had been a bargain. On one road he took an enemy king, four generals and ten thousand heads. The family is True Bone now. The rank opens most doors in the capital. It opens the best ones least.
[3] ¶ He is young and polite and so used to being the Gaya boy in the room that he apologises before anyone has accused him of anything. He sits a horse better than he sits a banquet.
[4] ¶ The best gate on the street belongs to Sukhuljong, the great king’s younger brother. Royal on every side. His daughter Manmyung is standing in it when Seohyun rides past. He looks. The histories, which don’t usually notice such things, record exactly how.
[5] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biography of Kim Yushin, part 1): At first, Seohyun saw on the road Manmyung, daughter of Sukhuljong, son of Galmun-wang Ipjong. His heart was glad, and he courted her with his eyes; and without waiting for a go-between, they came together.❞
[6] ── SCENE: The Gate ──
[7] ¶ The first time, he looks and keeps riding and nearly puts his horse into a charcoal cart. The second time he has an errand ready at the far end of the street, which does not exist. By the third the errand has run out, and he is only a man on a horse going the wrong way slowly.
[8] Manmyung’s maid: Agassi. It’s him again. / Same horse. Same— he’s pretending he isn’t looking.
[9] Manmyung: He’s terrible at it. / Don’t look. …No, look. I want to see what he does.
[10] ¶ Then she does something nobody on that street has seen a Sacred Bone daughter do. She steps down off the threshold into the dust.
[11] Manmyung: You’ve ridden past this gate three times today. / Is the road that bad, or are you lost?
[12] Kim Seohyun: I— the horse— / …It’s lost. I’m only on it.
[13] Manmyung: It looked fine the first time. / Nearly ate a charcoal cart. But fine.
[14] Kim Seohyun: That was— the cart was in the wrong— / Kim Seohyun. That’s— I should have said that first. Is it rude? I don’t know the rule for this.
[15] Manmyung: There isn’t one. That’s why it’s fun. / And I know who you are. Everyone on this street knows who you are.
[16] Kim Seohyun: …Ah. / The Gaya one.
[17] Manmyung: The one with the nice horse. / Then let it get lost again tomorrow. Same hour.
[18] Manmyung’s maid: Agassi—!
[19] ── SCENE: Getting Lost ──
[20] ¶ It gets lost every day for a season. The maid starts timing her errands by it. The charcoal man learns to pull over. Nobody sends a matchmaker, because a matchmaker would have to walk into Sukhuljong’s hall and say the word _Gaya_ out loud.
[21] ¶ By the end of summer they have stopped pretending about the horse. He leaves it at the bottom of the lane and walks up, and she talks to him through the side gate with the bar still down, because a gate with the bar down is technically closed.
[22] Manmyung: You’re late. / The horse?
[23] Kim Seohyun: The horse is fine. The horse is better than me. / They kept us at the Ministry. There’s talk of a posting.
[24] Manmyung: Where?
[25] Kim Seohyun: They haven’t said. North, probably. They send Gaya men north. / Somewhere with a lot of Goguryeo and not much—
[26] Manmyung: Not much me.
[27] Kim Seohyun: …I was going to say not much rice.
[28] Manmyung: Liar.
[29] ¶ Then she lifts the bar. Nobody on that street has seen a Sacred Bone daughter lift her own bar, either.
[30] Manmyung: Come in. / Not the front, idiot. The mulberry shed. Nobody goes in there after dark.
[31] Kim Seohyun: Agassi, I— your father— if anyone— / There are rules for this. I don’t know them, but there are—
[32] Manmyung: Then they’ll have something to talk about besides your horse.
[33] ¶ The shed smells of leaves and silkworms. She has his collar open before he has finished apologising for it. He is a careful man, and she is not a careful woman, and somewhere past midnight he stops being careful too.
[34] Kim Seohyun: That was— I should have— a go-between, a proper— / Your father should have been asked first.
[35] Manmyung: Shh. You talk a lot for a man with no shirt on. / Same hour tomorrow. Bring the horse, so it looks like an errand.
[36] ¶ He comes the next night, and the next. A go-between would have taken a season. They do not have a season. Some nights they barely have the walk up from the lane.
[37] ¶ The posting comes in the autumn: governor of **Manno**, a county far up the Goguryeo road, a wooden wall and a granary and a great many hills that change hands. He comes to the side gate with the seal still in his sleeve.
[38] Kim Seohyun: Manno. / It’s— a long way. Ten days if the passes are open. The house is small. I haven’t seen it, but they said small, and the way they said it— / I’m asking badly. I’m asking if you would—
[39] Manmyung: Yes.
[40] Kim Seohyun: —come with— I haven’t finished.
[41] Manmyung: Then finish. It’s still yes.
[42] ¶ The maid tells nobody. The charcoal man tells everybody. Her father knows by the next morning.
[43] ── SCENE: Sukhuljong’s Hall ──
[44] ¶ Sukhuljong takes the news sitting down, the way he takes most things, without looking up from his cup. He is a king’s son and a king’s brother, and he has never once in his life been the one left standing.
[45] Kim Sukhuljong: Muryuk’s boy. / The one whose grandfather carried his country here in a box and set it on the floor in front of my grandfather. / Him?
[46] Manmyung: His father kept his sword, Father. / You keep a gate.
[47] Kim Sukhuljong: A Gaya chair in a Kim hall. / Every guest who came would sit on it just to hear it creak. / Then you can look at the gate from the inside.
[48] Manmyung: You can’t keep me in a room forever.
[49] Kim Sukhuljong: I don’t need forever. / I need until he leaves for Manno.
[50] Manmyung: It was me, you know. Not him. He’d still be apologising to the horse. / I lifted the bar. Every night.
[51] Kim Sukhuljong: Take her to the back house.
[52] ¶ He shuts her in a house apart at the back of the compound and sets men on the door. Surabol has a word for what the two of them did, and it is not a polite one, and for a few weeks it is the only thing the city talks about.
[53] ── SCENE: The House Apart ──
[54] ¶ The guards are two cousins off one of Sukhuljong’s farms, chosen because they cannot be bribed and cannot read, and by the fourth night they have run out of things to say to each other.
[55] First guard: You think he’ll come?
[56] Second guard: The Gaya one? He says sorry to his own horse. / He’s not coming over a wall.
[57] First guard: I heard he leaves for the north day after tomorrow. First light.
[58] Second guard: Good. Then we go home.
[59] ¶ Inside, Manmyung has stopped eating to make a point and started again because the point was only hurting her. She has counted the boards in the ceiling. At the foot of the back wall, where the drain runs out, there is a gap, and she has been looking at it for three days the way her father looks at furniture.
[60] ¶ On the last night it storms. Lightning comes down on the door itself, and the guards do what men do when the sky picks out the house they are guarding, which is run. In the noise Manmyung goes out through a gap in the wall so low that she has to crawl, in her good silk, in the mud.
[61] Second guard: Heaven— it hit the door, it hit the DOOR—
[62] First guard: Leave it! It’s burning, leave the door, leave it—
[63] ¶ He is at the bottom of the lane with two horses, because he has been there every one of the four nights, in case. He sees a shape come out of the drain on its elbows, stand up and walk toward him through the rain like a woman going to market.
[64] Manmyung: Don’t— don’t look at the dress. / Is the horse lost tonight?
[65] Kim Seohyun: You— the lightning— are you hurt? Your hands—
[66] Manmyung: My hands are fine. Answer the question.
[67] Kim Seohyun: …No. / Tonight it knows exactly where it’s going.
[68] ¶ She kisses him before he can get her on the horse. Hard, in the rain, with drain-mud on her chin and both hands in his hair. The horses wait like men who have seen this before.
[69] Manmyung: …There. Now we can go.
[70] ¶ They ride north in the rain. Behind them, two cousins are trying to explain a door to Sukhuljong.
[71] ── SCENE: Manno ──
[72] ¶ Manno is a wooden wall, a granary, a county office with a leaking roof, and hills that have changed hands more often than the clerks can keep up with. She learns the granary. He learns the hills. Neither of them learns to cook, and by the second month the clerk’s wife has taken pity on them.
[73] ¶ The county house has one room with a door that shuts. The clerks learn not to knock before noon.
[74] ¶ He has a dream on a _gyeongjin_ night and tells nobody for three weeks, because a Gaya man who dreams of stars coming down on him does not say so in a county office. Then, on a _sinchuk_ night, she sits up in the dark and shakes him.
[75] Manmyung: Wake up. Wake up, I had— there was a boy. / In gold. Armour, all gold. He came in on a cloud, right into the hall, through the door like he owned the house. He looked at me.
[76] Kim Seohyun: …I had one too. Three weeks ago. / Two stars. A red one and a yellow one. They came down on me. Not on the house. On me.
[77] Manmyung: Three weeks. / Stars fell on you and you didn’t tell me for three weeks.
[78] Kim Seohyun: I thought it might be the soup.
[79] Manmyung: Pfft— the soup— / Come here, you. Come here.
[80] ¶ She is with child by spring. She is still with child the following spring, and the clerk’s wife, who has delivered half the county, stops coming to check and starts coming to stare.
[81] ¶ Word reaches Surabol before the spring rains do. A Sacred Bone daughter, with child, in a county house, and no wedding anyone was invited to. The city has been waiting for exactly this. Three banquets in a row talk about nothing else.
[82] Kim Seohyun: They’re saying things in Surabol. About you. About— there was no wedding, and now—
[83] Manmyung: Let them. They’re only saying what we did. / And we did it very well.
[84] The clerk’s wife: Twenty months, my lady. / I’ve had cows do it faster. / Either that child is something, or somebody counted wrong at the start, and I won’t say which. You’re the governor’s.
[85] Manmyung: Say it. I want to hear you say it.
[86] The clerk’s wife: …The child’s something.
[87] ¶ The boy is born in the county house at Manno. The clerk’s wife turns him over to wash him. She stops with the cloth in her hand.
[88] The clerk’s wife: My lady. His back. / Look— there. There’s seven. Like someone pressed them in with a thumb.
[89] Kim Seohyun: Seven what?
[90] The clerk’s wife: Stars, sir. The Dipper. On a baby. / I’m going to sit down.
[91] Manmyung: Sit, then. Sit. / And his eyes are some grandmother’s, a long way back. Seohyun says there was a boat.
[92] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Marvels — Kim Yushin): Lord Yushin was born in the _eulmyo_ year, the seventeenth of King Jinpyeong. He was endowed with the essence of the Seven Luminaries, and so his back bore a pattern of seven stars; and there were many other wonders about him.❞
[93] ¶ Naming him takes longer than carrying him did.
[94] Kim Seohyun: Gyeongjin. / I want to call him for the night I dreamed. That’s where he came from.
[95] Manmyung: You can’t name a child after a day. / Even I know that, and I ran away from all my tutors.
[96] Kim Seohyun: I know. I know. / But _gyeong_, written down, looks like _yu_. And _jin_, said quickly, is nearly _sin_. / And there was a man in the old books. A scholar. Yu Xin. A good man, they say. / So it isn’t a day. It’s a scholar. Nobody can say anything.
[97] Manmyung: You’ve been working on this for months.
[98] Kim Seohyun: …Twenty.
[99] ¶ They bury the afterbirth on the high hill behind the county, the way you do with a child you mean to keep, and the hill keeps the name.
[100] Manmyung: Yushin. / Say it to my father, next time you’re in Surabol. Say it at his gate.
[101] Kim Seohyun: …He won’t open it.
[102] Manmyung: Then say it louder.
[103] ── SCENE: The Name at the Gate ──
[104] ¶ A few weeks after the birth he rides to Surabol and says the name at Sukhuljong’s gate, loudly, to a street that has stopped to listen. The gate does not open. A steward comes out instead.
[105] Sukhuljong’s steward: His lordship is unwell. / He expects to be unwell for some years. He asked me to say it in exactly those words.
[106] Kim Seohyun: Tell him— / Tell him the boy has his mother’s mouth. / He’ll know what that means.
[107] Sukhuljong’s steward: …I’ll tell him, sir. / He won’t like it.
[108] ── SCENE: The Spring ──
[109] ¶ He rides home the long way because he does not want to arrive yet. The road goes over a ridge beyond the city that nobody uses, and by noon he wants water more than he has ever wanted a shrine. When heat breathes out of the hillside he calls it a spring and gets down.
[110] ¶ Under the hill three sisters keep the heat in the stone, the water in the dark and the moss on the roots: **Golhwa**, **Hyullé**, and **Narim**, the eldest, who also keeps the rules. They have gone centuries without a man coming down to them, and the hill has just told them about hooves on the road.
[111] Golhwa: Hooves! Unni. Unni, hooves. Someone stopped.
[112] Narim: Someone always stops. They drink, they piss in the stream, they leave.
[113] Hyullé: …This one’s crying a little.
[114] Golhwa: Crying? Let me see— move your elbow—
[115] Golhwa: Fox. Let’s be a fox. Foxes are fun.
[116] Hyullé: A grandmother. Then he drinks and bows and goes, and nobody… nobody gets hurt.
[117] Narim: Try both. Then I pick.
[118] ¶ They try both. The fox frightens the horse. The grandmother makes him kneel and offer her his waterskin with both hands, which is so polite that Golhwa groans out loud through the rock. Narim picks the last face herself: three young women in white jeogori over moss-green and ember and pale water-blue, sitting on the far rock as if they had always been there.
[119] ¶ He is still calling it a spring when the ground gives under his boot. He comes down through warm dark into a bowl of black water under stone and stands up coughing in a cloud of steam, soaked to the skin, his sword still somehow in his hand.
[120] Kim Seohyun: Who— forgive me— who lives here? / I was looking for water. There was an old woman just now, up there—
[121] Hyullé: …That was me. Sorry.
[122] Narim: You found your water. All of it at once. / Put the sword down, please. You’ll cut the steam.
[123] Golhwa: Hi. I’m Golhwa. That’s unni. That’s Hyullé, she won’t say hello unless you look at her first. / What’s your name? Say it slow.
[124] Kim Seohyun: Kim. Kim Seohyun. / Are you… I mean. People?
[125] ¶ At the surname all three of them go quiet. _Kim_ is the sound their own steam makes coming off the water, and nobody has ever said it to them as a name.
[126] Golhwa: Kim. / Say it again. No, I heard you. It just… sticks.
[127] Narim: Kim. / …Then the house rules apply. Golhwa. Chin.
[128] ¶ Golhwa is across the pool before he can step back, a wet hand under his jaw, turning his face to the light like a horse trader.
[129] Golhwa: Smooth. Shaved this morning? For who— oh. For the gate. Poor thing. / Chin passes, unni.
[130] Narim: Second rule. Nobody stands in this water dressed. / The steam doesn’t talk to cloth.
[131] Kim Seohyun: I— I have a wife. She’s— we have a son, he’s— / I’m sorry. I should have said that first.
[132] Golhwa: We didn’t ask about her.
[133] Hyullé: …You can turn around. We won’t— we won’t look.
[134] Golhwa: Speak for yourself.
[135] ¶ He turns his back, takes off the wet clothes and folds them badly on a rock, because he does not know what else to do with his hands. Hyullé does not look, mostly. Golhwa does not pretend. Narim waits until he is in the water to the chest and then lets out a breath, which nobody remarks on.
[136] Narim: Today we are the mouths the hill uses when it gets tired of being stone. / Ask it one thing, Kim. From the water. Once.
[137] ¶ He thinks of the gate. He thinks of a girl crawling through a hole in a wall in her good silk.
[138] Kim Seohyun: I have a son. A few weeks old. / My wife’s father won’t say his name. I stood at his gate this morning and said it for him, and— / I don’t know what to ask for him. I don’t know what you ask for a boy like that.
[139] ¶ Their eyes go solid, green and cyan and ember, and the cave stops being funny.
[140] The Hill: The child will be the measure two countries cannot share. / They will call him a blade and mean a border. / When they say he was never of them, the blade will still be Kim. / He will cut more than he is given. Don’t ask who bleeds.
[141] ¶ Narim puts a river stone in his hand, ordinary and grey and too warm for the cave.
[142] Narim: Keep it in your sleeve. / When it’s warm, come back. Same road, same water. One question. / When you’re too old to climb, send the boy.
[143] Golhwa: Shaved.
[144] Kim Seohyun: …Can I tell his mother?
[145] Golhwa: Tell her it was a spring. / Everybody says that.
[146] ── SCENE: Home to Manno ──
[147] ¶ He rides north with a stone in his sleeve that will not cool. At Manno, Manmyung is sitting up with the baby in the lamplight, and she asks him where he has been all day, and he tells her he found a spring.
[148] Manmyung: A spring. / …You’re smiling like a man who found three.
[149] Kim Seohyun: …It was a very good spring.
[150] Manmyung: Mm. / Your hair’s wet. It hasn’t rained in a week.
[151] ── SCENE: Fifteen ──
[152] ¶ The boy grows up at the edge of things, in county houses on the northern road. There’s a younger brother, and two little sisters the house calls by baby names. They’ll grow up to cause a great deal of trouble over a skirt. One of them is Munhee.
[153] ¶ At fifteen he is made a hwarang, and the boys who follow him start calling themselves the Dragon-Flower Band. Seohyun hears it from a clerk before he hears it from his son.
[154] ¶ The morning Yushin leaves for Surabol, his father stops him at the gate of the county house to look at his headband.
[155] Kim Seohyun: You’ve got it on crooked.
[156] Kim Yushin: It’s fine, Father.
[157] Kim Seohyun: It’s crooked. Hold still. / In Surabol they’ll look at the headband before they look at you. They’ll look for anything.
[158] Kim Yushin: Because we’re Gaya.
[159] Kim Seohyun: …Because you’re new. / Mostly because you’re new.
[160] ¶ He reties it with both hands, too tight, and then does it a third time. Manmyung watches from the doorway and lets him.
[161] Manmyung: Let him go. He’ll be late for his own band.
[162] Kim Yushin: Mother—
[163] Manmyung: And stop at your grandfather’s gate on the way. / Don’t knock. Just let them see you.
[164] ── SCENE: Daeyang ──
[165] ¶ Seohyun rises the way a Gaya man rises in the capital. One rank at a time, each signed by someone who remembers the box. By the end he is third rank in the kingdom. He governs the march that faces the enemy, from the fortress at Daeya.
[166] ¶ In the evenings he walks the wall at Daeya. Baekje is a line of hills to the west that the sun goes down behind.
[167] A Daeya officer: They say this wall can’t be taken, sir.
[168] Kim Seohyun: They say that about— every wall, I think. I’ve heard it about four. / Just— keep the granary dry. And know whose hands the keys are in. / My wife ran the granary at Manno. She’d tell you the same. She’d tell you better.
[169] ¶ The histories do not record the year he died, only how high he got. He climbs the ridge beyond the city whenever the stone in his sleeve is warm, shaved every time, until the climb is too much for him. Then the stone goes to his son. The boy with seven stars on his back finds the same water on his own and bathes in it for thirty years, and the stone in his sleeve stays cold the whole time, as if the hill were waiting for a better question.
[170] ¶ **Ninth morning, before light. The stone in his son’s sleeve is warm at last. Down Yushin goes, to the water…!**
